top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Melitz, firm heterogeneity and selection in trade) is the strongest case under one common standard: a distinct, mature discovery whose specific credited mechanism has been tested directly. Selection into exporting and reallocation across firms generate predictions that have been checked on firm-level customs and production data for over twenty years. The credit set is short and fits the discovery. Support counts are not merit and played no part. The case has limits. Exporter facts were documented before the model, so part of the empirical fit is accommodation of known facts, and the evidence supports the qualitative mechanism better than any welfare magnitude. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have serious claims outside the credited names. The 2008 prize overlap is a committee judgement, and I read firm selection as a distinct, later step. The citation should name the selection and reallocation mechanism, not a size of gains. P004 (Kiyotaki and Moore) ranks second because its attribution is the cleanest but direct validation of the collateral channel is weaker. P003 ranks third because its identification is strong but its boundary between discoveries is unresolved. P002 ranks fourth because its influence is large but the credit is diffuse and the credited building blocks are not clearly confirmed apart from the framework. No award ranks last, since each proposal is a scientifically serious candidate.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for the credited names. Melitz, Helpman, Redding, Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are not among my listed co-authors or institutional contacts. I disclose an SSE affiliation shared with committee members Friberg and Strömberg, and long co-authorship with Magnus Johannesson, a former committee member. My metascience background may lead me to overweight direct empirical validation. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
